steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Elias Morland had tended the Farhaven Light for so long that his name had become part of the wind-worn stone. Carved on the brass plaque fastened beside the door, it greeted every soul who ever climbed the switch-back stairs from the harbor: KEEPER ELIAS MORLAND, 1978—  

Yet Farhaven rarely saw visitors. The lighthouse stood on Dragontooth Point, a spine of basalt cliffs where green Atlantic swells battered themselves into lace. Supply trawlers ventured close only when skies were calm, and calm skies were a courtesy seldom granted.

Elias loved the solitude; or rather, he had grown into it the way vines grow into trellis, inseparable from its framework. Each dawn he rose before the gulls, brewed coffee strong enough to etch patterns on the mug, then wound the great clockwork drum that turned the lantern. He oiled gears, polished prisms, and with practiced palms checked every chimney draft that carried heat away from the incandescent mantle.

On Thursday mornings, at precisely ten, Elias performed “the reading.” No one required it; no manual listed it. Nevertheless he did it, standing in the lantern room with a battered leather volume of sea logs collected by keepers long dead. He opened a random page and read aloud: storms weathered, ships saved, lantern failures averted at the last second. The Fresnel lenses scattered his voice into shivering octagons of light that danced across the iron walls. In this way, he imagined the past keepers kept him company, listening from the brass rails of memory.

One November dusk, the barometer performed a stunt he had seen only once before: it plummeted so fast the needle blurred. Horizons vanished under iron-colored curtains. Elias lit the lamp early, beams piercing sleet like golden pikes. The storm screeched against the gallery glass; wind tugged at the doors, salt frothed through the keyholes. He tied himself to a ringbolt in the wall and waited.

Through the strobing dark he glimpsed a cargo vessel pitching starboard, her running lights askew. She was off course, flirting with Dragontooth’s submerged teeth. Elias seized the foghorn lever and pumped rhythmic blasts— three longs, one short— danger, turn away. The ship answered twice: distress. Electricity failed; the lamp guttered. For one panicked instant, the staircase behind him felt like the gullet of some whale, ready to swallow light and life both.

He struck a match, found the emergency mantle, and with trembling fingers coaxed a new flame into bloom. Glass steamed with frost; gears ground back to motion. The lantern flared, a second sunrise. Far below, the vessel’s bow swung laboriously, missing the outer reef by a margin so slim that Elias later measured it in heartbeats rather than meters. When her silhouette finally slipped beyond horizon, relief crashed over him as fiercely as the sea.

Afterward, exhaustion draped his shoulders. He brewed more coffee, black as the night he’d just bested, and resumed his rounds. Thunder rolled away; dawn smeared orange on slate clouds. Gulls returned to bicker above the surf, indifferent heralds of survival.

At ten sharp, he climbed to the lantern room for the reading. The leather logbook opened of its own accord, pages curling like petals. Elias cleared his throat, but before sound emerged he noticed fresh ink glistening where there had been none:  

“November 12. Gale force wind. Light lost, relit. Cargo ship Takoma diverted. Keeper E.M. on watch.”

His pen lay capped in his pocket; no one else could have written it. Wind, perhaps, had turned the page— yet the entry rested on a sheet that bore yesterday’s date, as though some unseen chronicler had already accounted for the night’s perils.

Elias smiled, a small, private upward curve. He read the entry aloud anyway, letting the words join the chorus of keepers past. The prisms scattered his voice, encoding memory into light. Somewhere out on the Atlantic, the Takoma’s crew poured coffee of their own, alive to greet another sunrise because a man alone on a cliff had refused to let darkness win.

When the reading ended, Elias closed the book, wound the clockwork, and gazed through glass beaded with dawn. Farhaven Light stood steady, its beam slicing morning mist— a slender promise that someone, somewhere, always keeps watch.
